claims.evidence: Direct observation by negative stain EM shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The length of the CtIP rod is broadly consistent with the predicted length of the coiled-coil domains.
claims.source: The length of the rod is broadly consistent with the predicted length of the coiled-coil domains, which suggests that the centre of the dumbbell is the site of the tetramerization interface as proposed in a previous model (Forment et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Comparison of measured rod length to predicted coiled-coil length, supported by citation to previous model.

claims.claim: CtIP 'tadpole' structures containing a single globular domain and a tail represent a dimeric form of the protein.
claims.source: In addition to the dumbbell structures, we less frequently observed structures that we call 'tadpoles' containing a single globular domain and a tail, which presumably represent a dimeric form of the protein formed during EM sample preparation and deposition (Figure 1B, α class; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Inference from observed morphology and comparison to tetrameric dumbbell structure.

claims.claim: AFM imaging of CtIP revealed five classes of particles (I–V) based on morphology and volume analysis.
claims.source: Broadly similar structures were observed by atomic force microscopy, although the sample appeared more heterogenous when applied to a mica surface, and five classes of particles were distinguished based on their volume and morphology (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: Direct observation and classification by AFM shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The largest class of CtIP particle (class V) has a relative volume consistent with a tetrameric species (~380 kDa).
claims.source: Finally, the largest class of particle contained up to four connected spots (class V). These different particles were associated with different volume profiles, with the largest particle class (class V) displaying a relative volume consistent with a tetrameric species (~380 kDa; Figure 1D) (Fuentes-Perez et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Volume measurement by AFM using fiducial marker method shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: CtIP R839A retained a tetrameric structure based on SEC-MALS analysis.
claims.source: The putative DNA binding mutant CtIPR839A (Andres et al., 2015), which disrupts the C-terminal RHR motif, retained a tetrameric structure based on SEC-MALS analysis (Figure 2A) and produced very similar results to the wild type protein in the AFM (Figure 2B and D).
claims.evidence: SEC-MALS analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: CtIP L27E ran as an apparently smaller particle in SEC-MALS with predicted molecular weights ranging from ~ 270 to 190 kDa.
claims.source: In contrast, the CtIPL27E mutant, which disrupts the N-terminal tetramerization interface (Davies et al., 2015), ran as an apparently smaller particle in SEC-MALS with predicted molecular weights across the peak ranging from ~ 270 to 190 kDa (most similar to a dimer molecular weight).
claims.evidence: SEC-MALS analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The CtIP L27E preparation was completely devoid of the largest class of particle (Class V) in AFM imaging.
claims.source: Importantly, when imaged using AFM, the CtIPL27E preparation was completely devoid of the largest class of particle (Class V; Figure 2C and E) which, in combination with the SEC-MALS results, suggests again that the class V particle represents tetrameric CtIP.
claims.evidence: AFM analysis shown in Figure 2C and E showing absence of class V particles.

claims.claim: The distance between the highest points of connected dots in CtIP particles was on the order of 30 nm with significant variability.
claims.source: For all particle classes, the distance between the highest points of the connected dots was on the order of 30 nm, although significant variability was observed consistent with flexibility in the connecting rod and/or the central region of the protein which is predicted to be disordered (see Figure 1—figure supplement 3 for examples and Discussion).
claims.evidence: Measurement from AFM height profiles shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: CtIP bound tightly to a forked DNA molecule containing a 25 bp duplex region flanked by 20 base ssDNA tails.
claims.source: CtIP bound tightly to a forked DNA molecule containing a 25 bp duplex region flanked by 20 base ssDNA tails (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: EMSA results shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: CtIP binding to completely single-stranded DNA was weaker than to forked DNA and resulted in more poorly defined complexes.
claims.source: The binding to a completely single-stranded DNA substrate was weaker and resulted in the formation of more poorly defined complexes in the gel.
claims.evidence: EMSA results comparing different DNA substrates.

claims.claim: CtIP binding to completely duplex DNA was considerably weaker than to forked DNA.
claims.source: Binding to a completely duplex DNA substrate was considerably weaker than to a forked substrate.
claims.evidence: EMSA results comparing different DNA substrates.

claims.claim: The equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd) for CtIP binding to HEX-labelled DNA fork is 16 nM.
claims.source: Firstly, we analysed directly the binding of CtIP to a HEX-labelled DNA fork using anisotropy (Figure 3D). The binding isotherm was well fit to a hyperbola yielding a value for the equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd) of 16 nM, which is somewhat tighter than suggested by using the semi-quantitative EMSA technique with the same substrate.
claims.evidence: Fluorescence anisotropy measurement shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: CtIP R839A has a Kd of 160 nM for DNA fork binding.
claims.source: Comparative analysis of the mutant proteins CtIPR839A and CtIPL27E using both assays showed that they were severely defective for DNA binding (Kd = 160 nM and 230 nM respectively) (Figure 3B–D).
claims.evidence: Fluorescence anisotropy measurement shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: CtIP L27E has a Kd of 230 nM for DNA fork binding.
claims.source: Comparative analysis of the mutant proteins CtIPR839A and CtIPL27E using both assays showed that they were severely defective for DNA binding (Kd = 160 nM and 230 nM respectively) (Figure 3B–D).
claims.evidence: Fluorescence anisotropy measurement shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Phosphatases have shown evidence for increased DNA binding affinity of CtIP.
claims.source: Phosphorylation is crucial for activation of CtIP during the S and G2 phases of the cell cycle. Somewhat surprisingly however, CtIP treated with phosphatases has shown evidence for an increased DNA binding affinity although this effect was not extensively investigated (Anand et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Anand et al., 2016.

claims.claim: CtIP as prepared from insect cells is hyper-phosphorylated.
claims.source: Analysis by mass spectrometry showed that our standard CtIP preparation is hyper-phosphorylated (see Figure 1—figure supplement 4 for details).
claims.evidence: Mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Dephosphorylated CtIP (CtIPλ) retained a tetrameric state.
claims.source: CtIPλ retained a tetrameric state (Figure 1A) and bound to forked DNA significantly more tightly than did untreated CtIP as judged crudely by EMSA (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: SEC-MALS analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Dephosphorylated CtIP displays > 10 fold tighter affinity for forked DNA compared to untreated CtIP.
claims.source: Furthermore, it displayed > 10 fold tighter affinity for forked DNA based on fluorescence anisotropy measurements (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: Fluorescence anisotropy measurements shown in Figure 4B comparing phosphorylated and dephosphorylated CtIP.

claims.claim: The Kd for dephosphorylated CtIP binding to DNA fork is 1.5 nM with a stoichiometry of 0.58 CtIP4 per DNA fork.
claims.source: The best fit to these data using the tight-binding equation (Equation 5) gave Kd = 1.5 nM and stoichiometry (n) = 0.58 CtIP4 per DNA fork.
claims.evidence: Fitting of fluorescence anisotropy data to tight-binding equation.

claims.claim: The binding stoichiometry of dephosphorylated CtIP to DNA fork was determined as 0.56 CtIP4 per DNA fork molecule by global fitting.
claims.source: The binding stoichiometry was determined as 0.56 CtIP4 per DNA fork molecule by global fitting of the data to the tight-binding equation (Equation 5).
claims.evidence: Global fitting of fluorescence anisotropy data at multiple DNA concentrations shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: A stoichiometry of 0.56 CtIP4 per DNA fork is equivalent to two DNA molecules bound to each CtIP tetramer at saturation.
claims.source: This is equivalent to two DNA molecules bound to each CtIP tetramer at saturation (assuming that our CtIP preparation is 100% active).
claims.evidence: Mathematical inference from measured stoichiometry.

claims.claim: Unlabelled fork DNA has an IC50 value of 55 nM in competition unbinding assays.
claims.source: In our first competition experiment, we found that titration of the unlabelled fork DNA against the reference probe yielded an IC50 value of 55 nM (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Competition unbinding assay shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Fully single-stranded DNA has an IC50 value of 314 nM and fully double-stranded DNA has an IC50 value of 392 nM in competition assays.
claims.source: In comparison, fully single- and double-stranded DNA substrates were relatively poor competitors (IC50 values of 314 nM and 392 nM respectively) in qualitative agreement with the EMSA analysis which had also shown a clear preference for forked DNA (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Competition unbinding assays shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The preference for forked DNA requires the presence of both 3′- and 5′- ssDNA overhangs (a Y-junction).
claims.source: Interestingly, this effect required the presence of both the 3′- and 5′- ssDNA overhangs in the fork (i.e. a Y-junction) as neither polarity overhang alone significantly improved the observed binding relative to duplex (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Competition assays comparing different DNA structures shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The IC50 value for CtIP binding to DNA was broadly similar for single- and double-stranded DNA in terms of total nucleotide concentration.
claims.source: We next titrated a variety of much larger competitor DNA molecules which differed in terms of their average length, topology, and whether they were single- or double-stranded (Figure 5D). In terms of the total nucleotide concentration, the IC50 value was broadly similar for single- and double-stranded DNA.
claims.evidence: Competition assays with various DNA substrates shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The IC50 for CtIP binding to DNA was largely unaffected by whether the DNA was circular, linearised or fragmented into many pieces.
claims.source: Moreover, the IC50 was largely unaffected by whether the DNA was circular, linearised or fragmented into many pieces.
claims.evidence: Competition assays comparing different DNA topologies.

claims.claim: CtIP does not bind preferentially to DNA ends compared to internal sites.
claims.source: This demonstrates that CtIP does not bind preferentially to DNA ends compared to internal sites because the efficacy of the competitor is independent of the total concentration of free DNA ends.
claims.evidence: Inference from competition assay results showing IC50 independence of DNA end concentration.

claims.claim: CtIP binding to single-stranded DNA was length dependent and very poor on substrates shorter than around 30 nucleotides.
claims.source: Further experiments with a range of short single-stranded oligonucleotides showed that binding was length dependent (in terms of absolute molecule concentrations) and very poor on substrates shorter than around 30 nucleotides (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Competition assays with oligonucleotides of varying length shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The addition of biotin labels alone to DNA termini had no significant effect or slightly weakened IC50 values.
claims.source: The addition of biotin labels alone to the termini of the DNA competitor molecules had no significant effect or slightly weakened the IC50 values.
claims.evidence: Competition assays comparing biotinylated and non-biotinylated DNA.

claims.claim: The binding of streptavidin to terminal biotin moieties dramatically increased the efficacy of DNA molecules as competitors for CtIP binding.
claims.source: However, the additional binding of streptavidin to the terminal biotin moieties dramatically increased the efficacy of the DNA molecules as competitors.
claims.evidence: Competition assays comparing biotinylated DNA with and without streptavidin.

claims.claim: A 45 bp duplex DNA with biotin:streptavidin blocks at both ends has an IC50 of 80 nM compared to 392 nM without blocks.
claims.source: For example, a fully duplex 45 base pair DNA molecule displayed an IC50 value of 392 nM and biotinylation of either one, or both of the ends, resulted in values of 413 and 448 nM respectively. However, the IC50 value reduced to 146 nM with a single biotin:streptavidin block and further to 80 nM with a biotin:streptavidin block at either end (compare the red bars in Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: Competition assays shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: The enhanced binding afforded by streptavidin blocking was apparent regardless of whether the biotin was placed at the 5' or 3' end of DNA strands.
claims.source: The enhanced binding afforded by streptavidin blocking was apparent regardless of whether the biotin moiety was placed at the 5' or 3' end of DNA strands (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Competition assays with different biotin positions shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The addition of streptavidin to DNA lacking biotin moieties had no effect on the observed IC50 value.
claims.source: Importantly, the addition of streptavidin to either single- or double-stranded competitor DNAs that lacked biotin moieties had no effect on the observed IC50 value (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: Control experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: When biotin was placed in the middle of a duplex DNA molecule, the IC50 value was weaker in the presence of streptavidin.
claims.source: In an attempt to address this, we also found that when a biotin was placed in the middle of a duplex DNA molecule, the IC50 value was now weaker in the presence of streptavidin (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Competition assays with internal biotin shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The association between DNA and Ku is severely inhibited by biotin:streptavidin end blocks.
claims.source: For example, the association between DNA and the NHEJ-factor Ku (with which CtIP competes to determine pathway choice in DSB repair) is seen to be severely inhibited by biotin:streptavidin end blocks in experiments analogous to those described above (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: Competition assays with Ku shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The DNA substrate used for AFM bridging experiments was homogenous, consisting virtually entirely of molecules with a single contour length.
claims.source: Initially we used AFM to image the DNA substrate alone (Figure 6A). The DNA was homogenous, consisting virtually entirely of molecules with a single contour length as would be expected (i.e. the DNA substrate was monomeric).
claims.evidence: AFM imaging and contour length analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The mean contour length measured for the control bare DNA substrate was 195 ± 22 nm.
claims.source: The length of the substrate DNA with single-strand overhangs is 587 bp, which we expect to be ~ 200 nm long based on a value of 0.34 nm/bp for B-DNA. In good agreement with this estimate, the mean contour length measured for the control bare DNA substrate was 195 ± 22 nm.
claims.evidence: AFM contour length measurement.

claims.claim: The percentage of DNA molecules above the threshold length (195 + 22 nm) is 4% in the no-protein control rising to about 30% with the highest concentrations of CtIP.
claims.source: Considering a threshold length of 195 + 22 nm (mean control length + SD), the percentage of molecules above this threshold is 4% in the 'no-protein' control experiment rising to about 30% in samples containing the highest concentrations of CtIP.
claims.evidence: Quantification of AFM contour length data.

claims.claim: About 7% of DNA molecules are bridged at exactly expected lengths (multiples of 195 nm within 2σ error) in samples containing wild type CtIP.
claims.source: In terms of the bridged molecules which are exactly the expected lengths (i.e. multiples of 195 nm within 2σ error) we see none whatsoever for the 'no protein' control, rising to ~ 7% in samples containing wild type CtIP (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: Quantification of bridged molecules shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: A range of intermolecular connections between two DNA duplexes was observed including end-to-end, end-to-centre and centre-to-centre.
claims.source: As would be expected based on our observation that the binding specificity is not strictly for ends, we saw a range of intermolecular connections between two DNA duplexes including end-to-end, end-to-centre and centre-to-centre (Figure 6B, zoomed-in panels).
claims.evidence: AFM imaging showing different bridging configurations in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Analysis of the height and width of bridging interfaces between DNA molecules provided evidence for additional mass interpreted as CtIP.
claims.source: Moreover, in many cases, analysis of the height and width of the bridging interfaces between DNA molecules provided evidence for additional mass which we interpret as CtIP (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1 for data).
claims.evidence: AFM height profile analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Dephosphorylated CtIP was more effective at bridging DNA molecules compared to wild type.
claims.source: We next compared the bridging ability of dephosphorylated CtIP and the two mutant proteins L27E and R839A, as well as performing an additional negative control with BSA in place of CtIP (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 4). In comparison to wild type, dephosphorylated CtIP was more effective at bridging DNA molecules.
claims.evidence: AFM bridging assays comparing different CtIP forms shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Both CtIP mutant proteins L27E and R839A were severely defective in DNA bridging.
claims.source: In contrast, both mutant proteins were severely defective in DNA bridging as would be expected based on their weak DNA binding affinities.
claims.evidence: AFM bridging assays shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: No bridging was observed in the no-protein control, although BSA showed a low level of apparent activity.
claims.source: On this measure, no bridging was observed in the 'no-protein' control, although a second negative control using BSA did show a low level of apparent activity.
claims.evidence: Control experiments in AFM bridging assays.

claims.claim: Bridging experiments with DNA lacking terminal ssDNA forks showed a reduced level of bridging.
claims.source: Interestingly, bridging experiments performed with a substrate that lacked the terminal ssDNA forks showed a reduced level of bridging, suggesting that the tighter DNA binding afforded by modifications to the DNA ends also facilitates DNA bridging as would be expected (data not shown).
claims.evidence: Unpublished AFM bridging experiments with different DNA substrates.

claims.claim: The dumbbell shape of CtIP is expected based on the hypothesis that CtIP adopts a 'dimer of dimers' arrangement.
claims.source: In this study we purified human CtIP protein and characterised its structure and DNA binding properties in vitro. The purified protein is tetrameric and adopts a striking 'dumbbell' architecture, which we have observed with both negative-stain EM and AFM. This shape is expected based on the hypothesis that CtIP adopts a 'dimer of dimers' arrangement, in which the tips of long N-terminal parallel coiled coils interact to form the tetrameric interface observed in crystal structures (Andres et al., 2015; Davies et al., 2015; Forment et al., 2015) (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: Inference based on crystal structures of N-terminal domain and observed dumbbell morphology.

claims.claim: A major DNA binding locus resides in the distal C-terminal domains of CtIP.
claims.source: Evidence that a major DNA binding locus resides in the distal C-terminal domains is provided by the inability of the R839A mutant to bind effectively to DNA, despite retaining a normal oligomeric state (this work; Andres et al., 2015; Figure 7).
claims.evidence: Inference from R839A mutant data showing loss of DNA binding without loss of tetramerization.

claims.claim: The globular structure of the C-terminal domains and the 2:4 stoichiometry of DNA to CtIP monomers implies a dimeric arrangement of the DNA binding domains.
claims.source: The globular structure of the C-terminal domains and the 2:4 stoichiometry of DNA to CtIP monomers implies a dimeric arrangement of the DNA binding domains.
claims.evidence: Inference from structural observations and stoichiometry measurements.

claims.claim: The C-terminal region of CtIP does not obviously resemble any known DNA binding domain despite the presence of the small 'RHR' motif.
claims.source: It will be of particular interest to determine a high-resolution structure for this region of the protein bound to DNA as, despite the presence of the small 'RHR' motif, this region of the protein does not obviously resemble any known DNA binding domain.
claims.evidence: Sequence analysis and comparison to known DNA binding domains.

claims.claim: The L27E mutation prevents assembly into a tetramer, DNA binding and DNA bridging.
claims.source: Mutation within the N-terminal coiled-coil domains prevents assembly into a tetramer, DNA binding and DNA bridging (Figures 2, 3 and 6).
claims.evidence: Data from multiple experiments with L27E mutant shown in Figures 2, 3, and 6.

claims.claim: The inability of L27E to bind to DNA implies that mutations in the coiled coils have effects on the distal DNA binding domains.
claims.source: The inability of L27E to bind to DNA implies that mutations in the coiled coils have effects on the distal DNA binding domains (see main text for discussion).
claims.evidence: Inference from L27E mutant data showing loss of DNA binding.

claims.claim: Wild type CtIP binds DNA without preference for ends per se and bridges DNA segments either intra- and inter-molecularly.
claims.source: Wild type CtIP binds DNA without preference for ends per se (i.e. internally) and bridges DNA segments either intra- and inter-molecularly (Figures 5 and 6, and the Figure Supplements).
claims.evidence: Data from competition assays and AFM bridging experiments shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claims.claim: CtIP may slide and capture DNA ends possessing forked structures or nucleoprotein conjugates because they prevent dissociation from the free ends.
claims.source: Based on the preferential binding to DNA with forked or blocked ends (Figure 5), we speculate that CtIP may then slide and capture DNA ends possessing forked structures or nucleoprotein conjugates, because they prevent dissociation from the free ends (see main text for discussion).
claims.evidence: Speculation based on observed preferential binding to complex DNA ends.

claims.claim: The mechanism by which modifications to DNA ends increase the affinity of CtIP for DNA could involve a 'slide and capture' mechanism.
claims.source: The mechanism by which modifications to DNA ends increase the affinity of CtIP for DNA remains to be determined. One simple possibility would be that CtIP interacts directly with the protein or nucleic acid conjugates that we have appended to our DNA substrates. However, we do not favour such a model: it is difficult to see how a direct protein-mediated interaction could recognise the fundamentally different types of ends that we have used in vitro or which must presumably be recognised in vivo. Alternatively, the protein might act via a 'slide and capture' mechanism in which the interaction is initially with internal sites with the DNA ends acting as exit sites.
claims.evidence: Speculation based on experimental observations and mechanistic reasoning.

claims.claim: Complex DNA ends would act to capture CtIP by disfavouring dissociation if the end is modified with any bulky blocking moiety.
claims.source: In that case the dissociation may be disfavoured if the end is modified with any bulky blocking moiety, including Y-junctions and nucleoprotein complexes, such that complex ends would act to capture CtIP (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: Speculation based on slide and capture model.

claims.claim: The localisation of CtIP at DSBs in vivo is likely mediated by proteins with which it interacts, including BRCA1-BARD1 and MRN, or by post-translational modifications.
claims.source: Presumably, the localisation of CtIP at DSBs in vivo is also mediated by the many other proteins with which it interacts, including the BRCA1-BARD1 complex and MRN, or by the post-translational modifications which they facilitate.
claims.evidence: Speculation based on known protein interactions and established knowledge.

claims.claim: The regulation of DSB repair factors by downregulation of DNA binding via post-translational modification is not unprecedented.
claims.source: Nevertheless, the regulation of DSB repair factors by downregulation of DNA binding via post-translational modification is certainly not unprecedented (Blanco et al., 2014; Honda et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies of other DSB repair factors.

claims.claim: Each CtIP tetramer can bind two DNA fork molecules.
claims.source: We found that each tetramer can bind two such DNA molecules.
claims.evidence: Stoichiometry determination from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claims.claim: The two DNA molecules bound by CtIP may bind to the opposing ends of the tetramer where a major DNA binding locus is formed by dimerization of the C-terminal domains.
claims.source: Given the dumbbell architecture that we have observed and the location of a key DNA binding motif in the distal C-terminus, we speculate that these two DNA molecules bind to the opposing ends of the tetramer, where a major DNA binding locus might be formed by dimerization of the C-terminal domains including the RHR motif.
claims.evidence: Speculation based on structural observations and stoichiometry data.

claims.claim: The CtIP arrangement may help to co-ordinate the repair and eventual re-joining of two DSBs.
claims.source: This arrangement may help to co-ordinate the repair and eventual re-joining of two DSBs (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: Speculation about functional implications of observed structure.

claims.claim: AFM experiments observed significant flexibility in the connecting rod between the globular domains of CtIP.
claims.source: In this respect, it is interesting to note that our AFM experiments observed significant flexibility in the connecting rod between the globular domains, which may help facilitate such co-ordination.
claims.evidence: AFM observations showing variable distances between globular domains.

claims.claim: CtIP bridging activity might help to tether the homology donor DNA in proximity to the broken DNA molecules to promote strand exchange.
claims.source: Consistent with this model, we also showed that CtIP was able to bridge DNA segments intermolecularly. Such a bridging activity might also help to tether the homology donor DNA in proximity to the broken DNA molecules to promote strand exchange.
claims.evidence: Speculation about functional implications of observed bridging activity.

claims.claim: CtIP may act as a binding platform for co-ordinating two ended DSBs with recruitment of signalling factors and assembly of a 'resectosome' complex.
claims.source: Given the very large number of reported CtIP interaction partners, it is possible that CtIP acts as a binding platform for co-ordinating two ended DSBs with the recruitment of signalling factors of the DNA damage response and for the assembly of a 'resectosome' complex to promote repair by recombination.
claims.evidence: Speculation based on known interaction partners and observed properties.

results.result: Human CtIP is a tetrameric protein with a dumbbell architecture consisting of polar globular domains connected by a ~30 nm central rod formed by coiled-coil domains. This structure was characterized by SEC-MALS (391 ± 23 kDa), negative stain EM, and AFM, revealing five particle classes with the largest (Class V) consistent with a tetramer (~380 kDa).
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C50-C60, and C99 provide converging evidence from multiple orthogonal techniques (SEC-MALS, EM, AFM) demonstrating the tetrameric state and dumbbell architecture. The molecular weight measurements are consistent with a tetramer, and direct visualization confirms the predicted structure. The L27E mutant data (C58-C59) provides additional validation by showing loss of Class V particles when tetramerization is disrupted.

results.result: Each CtIP tetramer binds two DNA fork molecules with high affinity. Fluorescence anisotropy experiments with dephosphorylated CtIP yielded a stoichiometry of 0.56-0.58 CtIP tetramers per DNA fork (Kd = 1.5 nM), equivalent to two DNA molecules per tetramer at saturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C71-C73, and C111 are well-supported by quantitative fluorescence anisotropy measurements using tight-binding conditions with multiple DNA concentrations. The stoichiometry determination is rigorous, employing global fitting to equation 5. The caveat that this assumes 100% active protein is appropriately noted.

results.result: CtIP bridges DNA molecules both intra- and inter-molecularly in trans. AFM experiments showed CtIP-dependent increase in DNA molecules with contour lengths equal to multiples of single DNA length (from 4% in controls to ~30% with CtIP, with ~7% at exact expected lengths). Dephosphorylated CtIP showed enhanced bridging, while L27E and R839A mutants were severely defective.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C88-C98 provide direct AFM visualization evidence for DNA bridging activity. The quantification shows clear CtIP-dependent effects, with appropriate controls (no protein, BSA). The observation of protein mass at bridging interfaces (C94) and various bridging configurations (C93) strengthen the conclusion. Mutant analysis (C95-C96) confirms specificity.

results.result: DNA binding by CtIP is potentiated >10-fold by dephosphorylation. Dephosphorylated CtIP (Kd = 1.5 nM) binds forked DNA with >10-fold higher affinity than hyperphosphorylated CtIP (Kd = 16 nM), while retaining tetrameric structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C67-C70 are supported by quantitative fluorescence anisotropy and EMSA data. Mass spectrometry confirms hyperphosphorylation of the as-prepared protein (C68). The effect is time-resolved (Figure 4—supplement 1), ruling out artifacts from buffer conditions. However, the specific phosphorylation sites responsible remain unidentified.

results.result: CtIP does not bind preferentially to DNA ends per se. Competition assays showed IC50 values were independent of DNA topology (circular, linear, or fragmented) and similar for single- and double-stranded DNA in terms of nucleotide concentration, demonstrating no preference for DNA ends over internal sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C77-C79 are well-supported by systematic competition unbinding assays comparing DNA substrates with different topologies and end densities. The independence of IC50 from DNA end concentration (C78-C79) provides strong evidence against end-specific binding. This is a surprising but well-documented finding.

results.result: CtIP affinity for DNA is increased by forked ssDNA overhangs at termini. Forked DNA (IC50 = 55 nM) binds ~7-fold better than duplex DNA (IC50 = 392 nM), requiring both 3' and 5' ssDNA overhangs (Y-junction), as neither polarity alone improved binding relative to duplex.
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C61-C63, C74-C76 are supported by both EMSA and quantitative competition assays. The requirement for both 3' and 5' overhangs (C76) is a specific structural requirement that strengthens the conclusion. The data consistently show preference for forked structures across multiple assay formats.

results.result: CtIP affinity for DNA is dramatically increased by nucleoprotein conjugates (biotin:streptavidin blocks) at DNA termini. Duplex DNA IC50 decreased from 392 nM to 80 nM with blocks at both ends. This effect required biotin at DNA ends (not internal positions) and was independent of strand polarity.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C81-C86 provide systematic evidence for enhanced binding with terminal protein blocks. Controls show biotin alone has no effect (C81), streptavidin without biotin has no effect (C85), and internal biotin weakens binding (C86). The effect is specific to terminal conjugates and independent of polarity (C84).

results.result: The R839A mutation in the C-terminal RHR motif severely impairs DNA binding (Kd = 160 nM vs 16 nM for WT) without affecting tetrameric structure, indicating a major DNA binding locus resides in the C-terminal domains. The L27E mutation prevents tetramerization, DNA binding (Kd = 230 nM), and DNA bridging.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 and C100, C103 are supported by SEC-MALS showing R839A retains tetrameric structure (C57) while losing DNA binding affinity (~10-fold reduction). L27E loses both tetramerization (C58-C59) and DNA binding. The separation of oligomerization and DNA binding defects in R839A provides strong evidence for C-terminal DNA binding domains.

results.result: The L27E mutation's inability to bind DNA implies that mutations in the N-terminal coiled coils affect the distal C-terminal DNA binding domains, suggesting long-range structural communication or architectural requirements for DNA binding.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 is an inference from the L27E data. While the observation that L27E loses both tetramerization and DNA binding is clear, the mechanism is uncertain. The authors acknowledge they see no cooperativity in binding and suggest the effect may be due to global architectural disruption rather than specific communication between domains. Alternative explanations are not ruled out.

results.result: CtIP binding to single-stranded DNA is length-dependent and very poor on substrates shorter than ~30 nucleotides, as shown by competition assays with oligonucleotides of varying length.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is supported by systematic competition assays with oligonucleotides of different lengths (Figure 5—supplement 3). This provides a minimum binding site size estimate, though the exact threshold and whether this reflects a single binding site or multiple contacts is not fully characterized.

results.result: The NHEJ factor Ku shows opposite behavior to CtIP: Ku binding to DNA is severely inhibited by biotin:streptavidin end blocks, contrasting with CtIP's enhanced binding under the same conditions.
results.evaluation: Claim C87 is supported by control experiments (Figure 5—supplement 4) showing that Ku, a known end-binding protein, is inhibited by terminal blocks. This validates the experimental approach and highlights the unusual properties of CtIP compared to conventional end-binding proteins.

results.result: The authors propose a 'slide and capture' mechanism where CtIP initially binds internal DNA sites and slides until captured at complex DNA ends (forks or nucleoprotein blocks) that prevent dissociation. This model explains the preferential binding to modified ends without requiring direct recognition of end structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 represent a speculative mechanistic model. While the model is consistent with the data (no end preference per se, but enhanced binding with terminal modifications), it is not directly tested. Alternative mechanisms (e.g., conformational changes upon encountering blocks) are not rigorously excluded. The authors appropriately present this as speculation.

results.result: The 2:4 stoichiometry of DNA to CtIP monomers and globular C-terminal structure implies a dimeric arrangement of DNA binding domains, with two DNA molecules potentially binding at opposing ends of the tetramer where C-terminal domains dimerize.
results.evaluation: Claims C101 and C112 are inferences from stoichiometry and structural data. While the 2:1 DNA:tetramer ratio is well-established, the precise arrangement of DNA binding sites is speculative. The dumbbell architecture supports the model of binding at opposing ends, but high-resolution structural data of DNA-bound complexes would be needed for confirmation.

results.result: The authors speculate that CtIP's architecture and bridging activity may coordinate repair of two DSBs, tether homology donor DNA, and serve as a platform for recruiting signaling factors and assembling a 'resectosome' complex, facilitated by flexibility in the connecting rod observed by AFM.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C116 are speculative functional interpretations. While the structural and biochemical data (bridging, 2:1 stoichiometry, flexibility) are consistent with these roles, direct evidence for these functions in vivo is not provided. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future work but are not demonstrated in this study.

results.result: The Introduction provides established background on DSB repair pathways, CtIP's role in HR and end resection, MRN-CtIP cooperation, controversy over CtIP nuclease activity, and limited prior structural information on CtIP N-terminal regions from yeast and human studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C49 represent background knowledge and literature citations that provide context for the study. These are appropriately cited and represent established knowledge in the field. The citations appear accurate based on the references provided, though detailed verification of each cited claim is beyond the scope of this review.

results.result: The equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd) for hyperphosphorylated CtIP binding to HEX-labeled DNA fork is 16 nM, as determined by fluorescence anisotropy fitted to a hyperbolic binding curve.
results.evaluation: Claim C64 is supported by direct fluorescence anisotropy measurements (Figure 3D). The Kd value is determined under standard binding conditions and represents the affinity of the as-prepared (hyperphosphorylated) protein. This serves as a baseline for comparison with dephosphorylated protein.

results.result: The C-terminal region of CtIP does not obviously resemble any known DNA binding domain despite containing the RHR motif, based on sequence analysis and comparison to known DNA binding domains.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 is supported by sequence analysis (implicit in the statement). The lack of recognizable DNA binding motifs makes the structural characterization of this region particularly important for future work, as noted by the authors. This is a knowledge-based claim that appears accurate.

results.result: The authors speculate that CtIP localization at DSBs in vivo is likely mediated by protein interactions (BRCA1-BARD1, MRN) and post-translational modifications, in addition to the DNA binding properties characterized in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claim C109 is a reasonable speculation based on established knowledge of CtIP's many interaction partners. The in vitro DNA binding properties alone may not fully explain in vivo localization, and the authors appropriately acknowledge the likely contribution of protein-protein interactions and PTMs.

results.result: Regulation of DSB repair factors by downregulation of DNA binding via post-translational modification is not unprecedented, as demonstrated for other repair factors in cited studies.
results.evaluation: Claim C110 is supported by citations to studies of other DSB repair factors (Blanco et al., 2014; Honda et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2016). This provides context for the counterintuitive finding that dephosphorylation enhances CtIP DNA binding despite phosphorylation being required for activation in vivo.
